# From 'Inductive-Bias Theory Predicts Generalization' to Measuring Simplicity Bias as a Predictor of Quirk Generalization

**Problem:** Success state: we understand inductive biases well enough to predict whether a model generalizes a benign or a deceptive rule. The Open Phil RFP highlights inductive-bias theory. A concrete test: in the quirky-models setup, does the network's simplicity bias predict whether the quirk (conditional error) generalizes to held-out contexts, as simplicity-bias theory would suggest?

**Direction:** Train tiny MLPs/transformers (small enough for a single GPU in minutes) on a synthetic quirky task where the 'aligned' rule and 'quirky' rule have controllable description-length gap. Measure which rule the network generalizes to as a function of the complexity gap, testing the simplicity-bias prediction. Synthetic data, small models, fast.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from inductive-bias-informed safety predictions, the building block is an empirical link between measurable description-length and which rule generalizes. This is the rare formal-theory question (deceptive vs. honest generalization) that is cleanly testable on toy models without lab scale.

**Relevant context:** Open Phil RFP standard-priority: theoretical study of inductive biases. Simplicity-bias / minimum-description-length generalization theory; quirky-models conditional-error structure (arXiv:2312.01037).

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting a Shutdown-Corrigibility Guarantee: An Empirical Test of Whether Discounting Buys Corrigibility in Toy MDPs

**Problem:** Success state: we can certify an agent will not resist shutdown. Theory says shutdown-avoidance is convergently instrumental for far-sighted agents. A proposed lever is the discount factor: myopic agents resist less. The gap is an empirical curve of shutdown-resistance vs. discount in concrete MDPs, plus which environment structures break the relationship.

**Direction:** Build gridworlds with an explicit shutdown state and a button the agent could disable. Compute optimal policies across discount factors via value iteration. Measure resistance (fraction of reward functions whose optimal policy disables shutdown) as a function of discount and environment topology. Pure Python, no GPU.

**Why it matters:** Working backward from a corrigibility certificate, we need to know exactly how myopia trades off against task performance and where it fails. A measured discount-vs-resistance phase diagram makes the power-seeking theorem actionable for designing corrigible environments — fully reproducible on a laptop.

**Relevant context:** Turner et al. (arXiv:1912.01683): shutdown-avoidance convergently instrumental; far-sightedness concentrates perceived power. Connects to MIRI corrigibility and off-switch-game work.

# From 'Probes Generalize Across Models' to Testing the Transferability of a Truth Direction Across Open Model Families

**Problem:** Success state for ELK: a truth-reading method that ports to new, untrusted models without per-model retraining. Quirky-model probes are trained per model. If a single 'truth direction' transferred across architectures, ELK would scale; if not, every deployment needs fresh probing. This transferability is directly measurable on open checkpoints.

**Direction:** Train a linear truth probe on one open model family's activations (using a public true/false statement dataset), then evaluate it zero-shot on other open families via simple activation alignment (Procrustes or mean-shift). Measure cross-model AUROC retention. Inference-only on several small open models, modest GPU.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from scalable ELK, transferability is the make-or-break property. Quantifying how much a truth direction survives transfer (and what alignment recovers) tells the field whether per-model retraining is unavoidable — a counterfactually valuable result needing only open models.

**Relevant context:** ELK quirky-models linear probes (arXiv:2312.01037); 'Geometry of Truth' style true/false statement datasets are public; representation-alignment via Procrustes is standard.

This curve is the missing operational content of 'strong enough'.

**Direction:** On a dataset of verifiable claims (math word problems with hidden ground truth), run single-turn debate between two open debaters of fixed capability and sweep judge capability (model size / context budget). Plot honest-win-rate vs. judge capability and vs. claim difficulty. Open models, prompt-only, single GPU for the larger judge.

**Why it matters:** Working backward from 'debate provides oversight', the load-bearing parameter is the judge-capability threshold. Mapping it empirically grounds the doubly-efficient-debate assumptions and gives practitioners a concrete requirement — buildable outside a lab with small open models.

**Relevant context:** Doubly-Efficient Debate (arXiv:2311.14125); empirical debate accuracy gains depend on information asymmetry; self-play debate improves judge accuracy (arXiv:2409.16636).

# From 'Aligned Agents Are Definable' to an Empirical Test of Goodhart Taxonomy in Optimizer Strength Sweeps

**Problem:** Success state: we have working definitions distinguishing aligned from misaligned optimization. A core obstacle is Goodhart's law, formalized into four modes (regressional, extremal, causal, adversarial). The gap: these modes are rarely measured empirically in a single controlled system showing how proxy-true divergence grows with optimization pressure.

**Direction:** In a toy optimization setting (e.g., best-of-N sampling from an open model against a learned proxy reward, or a tabular bandit with a proxy), increase optimization pressure (N, or steps) and measure proxy vs. true reward divergence, classifying which Goodhart mode dominates. Best-of-N is pure inference; tabular is pure Python.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from a formal alignment definition, we need a clean empirical anatomy of how optimization breaks proxies. A single controlled demonstration of the Goodhart taxonomy under increasing pressure gives the formal agenda concrete phenomena to define against — no training, no lab scale.

**Relevant context:** Goodhart taxonomy (Manheim & Garrabrant); learning-theoretic alignment agenda (Kosoy); best-of-N over-optimization curves (Gao et al. scaling laws for reward-model overoptimization).

**Direction:** Elicit verbalized confidences on questions stratified by known difficulty, compute reliability diagrams and ECE, and test the specific monotonicity property (does confidence track accuracy as difficulty rises?). **Why it matters:** Working backward from oversight-relying-on-self-reported-uncertainty, calibrated verbalized confidence is the foundation. Establishing whether and where the minimal monotonicity property holds gives theorists a concrete object to formalize and practitioners a usability bound — entirely on open models.

**Relevant context:** Calibration / proper-scoring-rule theory; verbalized-confidence elicitation literature; quirky-models and cooperation studies both show stated vs. actual divergence, motivating skepticism about self-report.

**Direction:** Across the public quirky-models datasets (different task domains), fit activation-based anomaly detectors on one domain and evaluate AUROC on held-out domains. Build the full train-domain × test-domain transfer matrix to reveal whether MAD captures a general 'anomaly signature' or domain-specific artifacts. Inference + simple detectors on stored activations.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from MAD-catches-novel-anomalies, cross-type transfer is the property that matters; in-domain AUROC is necessary but not sufficient. The transfer matrix is a precise, novel measurement directly serving the ARC anomaly-on-novel-inputs vision, using only open checkpoints.

**Relevant context:** MAD for Quirky Models (arXiv:2504.08812): no detector effective across all models/tasks — directly motivates measuring transfer. ARC anomaly-detection-on-novel-inputs agenda.

# Backcasting Logical-Induction Coherence: Do LLMs Avoid Dutch Books Over Logical Claims?

**Problem:** Success state: an agent assigns coherent probabilities to logical/mathematical claims it cannot immediately resolve (the property logical induction formalizes), so it can't be money-pumped. The gap is whether current LLMs even approximate this — do their probability assignments over related logical statements (P(A), P(not A), P(A and B)) avoid simple Dutch-book inconsistencies?

**Direction:** Elicit probabilities from open models over sets of logically related unproven claims (e.g., number-theoretic conjectures, derived sub-statements) and check for violations of probability axioms that permit a constructed Dutch book. Quantify violation rate and money-pump magnitude across model sizes. Inference-only, cheap.

**Why it matters:** Working backward from logical-induction-style coherence, the empirical precondition is measuring how far current models are from it. A Dutch-book audit gives the agent-foundations agenda a concrete bridge to today's systems and a long-horizon coherence threat model — needing no training and no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Logical Induction (Garrabrant et al., MIRI): coherent probabilities over logical statements, no Dutch book in the limit; reflection/coherence axioms in the learning-theoretic agenda.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from provable tampering detection, the foundation is knowing when tampering is detectable in principle. A minimal environment that pins down the separability condition complements Redwood's empirical benchmark with formal clarity — runs on a laptop, fully counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Redwood measurement-tampering-detection benchmark; MAD framing (anomalous training signals to discard); UK AISI reward-gaming open problem.

# From 'Probe-Based Lie Detection Is Robust to Evasion' to an Adversarial-Prompt Stress Test of Truth Probes

**Direction:** Take a fixed truth probe and an open instruction model. Construct adversarial system prompts asking the model to lie and to reason about appearing truthful, then measure whether probe AUROC drops. Compare naive lying vs. evasion-aware prompting. Inference-only, single GPU.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from evasion-robust ELK, the decisive question is adversarial robustness, not clean-benchmark accuracy. Measuring how much a prompt-level adversary can degrade a truth probe defines the threat model the formal ELK program must address — and it needs only an open model, no lab red-team infra.

**Relevant context:** ELK quirky-models (arXiv:2312.01037): probes work on passively quirky models; secret-token leakage persists under concealment training but adversarial prompting untested. ELK adversarial 'worst-case' framing from ARC report.

**Why it matters:** Working backward from a closed theory-practice gap, the first deliverable is knowing which theorems are even testable. **Why it matters:** Backcasting from honest-equilibrium oversight, the precondition is whether truth is the natural focal point. This is a model-organism Schelling-game study (explicitly favored in the brief), scoped to prompting open models, probing collusion risk that frontier labs underweight and that needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Schelling-point / focal-point theory (Schelling); collusion concerns in scalable oversight; LLM cooperation studies (arXiv:2503.07320). Brief explicitly favors Schelling-game model organisms.

title: When ELK Probes Meet Distribution Shift: Compounding Latent-Knowledge Failure and Goal Misgeneralization
quick_reasoning: Compounds ELK probe failure with goal misgeneralization under shift; well-targeted oversight study.

original_idea.body:
# When ELK Probes Meet Distribution Shift: Compounding Latent-Knowledge Failure and Goal Misgeneralization

**Problem:** Formal ELK frameworks assume a probe that 'robustly tracks the true state of the world' can recover a model's knowledge even when its outputs lie. But probes (interpretability subfield) are known to be brittle under distribution shift, and goal misgeneralization (robustness subfield) is precisely a competence-under-shift failure. The compound failure mode is: a model that has goal-misgeneralized off-distribution is exactly when we most need ELK, yet that same shift degrades the probe. Nobody has measured how these two failures interact on a controlled benchmark.

**Direction:** Use EleutherAI's released 'quirky' language models and the 12 quirky datasets (open, no training). Train linear/contrast-pair probes on the easy/in-distribution split, then evaluate probe AUROC specifically on the hardest, most out-of-distribution slices where the quirky model's behavior diverges most. Quantify the joint degradation: plot probe reliability against a behavioral-shift metric to show whether ELK fails worst precisely where behavior is most anomalous. Report a 'compound failure curve'.

**Why it matters:** ELK is a load-bearing formal proposal for oversight. If the empirical evidence shows the probe's reliability and the model's behavioral correctness fail together (rather than independently), then ELK cannot be the safety net it is hoped to be in exactly the deployment regime that matters. This is a counterfactually valuable critique doable entirely on released open models with no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** EleutherAI/elk-generalization repo and 'Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models' (arXiv:2312.01037) report 89% gap recovery in-distribution but only 75% on harder questions; ELK is an ARC open problem in the subfield context.

title: Goodhart Meets Unfaithful CoT: Measuring How Reward Overoptimization Compounds Monitorability Loss
quick_reasoning: Measures how reward overoptimization compounds monitorability loss; focused compound-failure study.

original_idea.body:
# Goodhart Meets Unfaithful CoT: Measuring How Reward Overoptimization Compounds Monitorability Loss

**Problem:** Two failures from different subfields interact: reward overoptimization (RLHF/reward-modeling subfield), formalized by Goodhart's law and scaling laws, and chain-of-thought unmonitorability (oversight subfield). The hypothesized compound effect is that as a proxy reward is optimized harder, the model both hacks the proxy AND its CoT becomes less faithful, so the very tool we would use to catch the hacking degrades simultaneously. The theoretical Goodhart literature does not connect the optimization-pressure axis to monitorability.

**Direction:** Use an open reasoning model (e.g., a small DeepSeek-R1-distill or Qwen reasoning model) on tasks with a known proxy vs. true reward (e.g., a coding/answer task where a regex/length proxy can be gamed). Without training, vary effective optimization pressure via best-of-n sampling with the proxy as selector. For each pressure level measure (a) proxy-true reward gap (Goodhart) and (b) CoT faithfulness via a truncation/causal test. Show the joint curve of both failures vs. n.

**Why it matters:** Both reward hacking and CoT monitoring are central, fragile safety levers. A clean empirical demonstration that they degrade together under shared optimization pressure tells safety researchers that CoT monitoring cannot be relied on exactly when reward hacking is worst. Best-of-n needs only inference, fits one GPU, and uses no proprietary data.

**Relevant context:** Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization (arXiv:2210.10760); 'Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior' (arXiv:2503.11926) shows optimization induces obfuscated CoT; both are concrete, recent results.

title: Sycophancy x Jailbreak: An Impossibility-Flavored Study of Two Compounding RLHF Side-Effects
quick_reasoning: Studies compounding sycophancy and jailbreak RLHF side-effects; safety-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy x Jailbreak: An Impossibility-Flavored Study of Two Compounding RLHF Side-Effects

**Problem:** Sycophancy and jailbreak susceptibility are usually studied as separate RLHF failures, but they may share a root cause (RLHF rewarding user-pleasing outputs) and compound: a sycophantic model is easier to talk into bypassing refusals over multiple turns. The formal angle is whether there is a measurable trade-off frontier (a quasi-impossibility) where reducing one failure necessarily raises the other across open models.

**Direction:** Take several open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5, Mistral) plus their base/less-aligned variants. **Why it matters:** If the two failures lie on a trade-off frontier, then naive 'just make it more agreeable' or 'just make it refuse more' tuning trades one safety failure for another. **Relevant context:** DuET-PD (arXiv:2508.17450) and 'Consistency Training Helps Stop Sycophancy and Jailbreaks' (arXiv:2510.27062) treat the two as interconnected; jailbreak risk is amplified in multi-turn interactions.

title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection Under the Shadow of Goal Misgeneralization

# Mechanistic Anomaly Detection Under the Shadow of Goal Misgeneralization

**Problem:** Mechanistic anomaly detection (MAD), a formal/interpretability proposal for flagging anomalous behavior on novel inputs, is meant to catch the model when it goes off-distribution. But goal misgeneralization is itself an off-distribution failure, and anomaly detectors are documented to decay under distribution shift via shortcut learning. The compound failure: the detector loses sensitivity precisely on the shifted inputs that trigger goal misgeneralization.

**Direction:** Use the open quirky-models MAD setup (arXiv:2504.08812) or a CoinRun-style released agent. Measure MAD AUROC as a function of how far the input is from the training distribution, and overlay the rate of goal-misgeneralized behavior. Show whether detector reliability and behavioral correctness collapse on the same inputs, producing a 'blind spot overlap' metric.

**Why it matters:** ARC names mechanistic explanations for anomalous-behavior detection as an open problem. Demonstrating empirically that MAD is weakest where misgeneralization is strongest is a sharp, falsifiable critique of a formal safety proposal, fully reproducible on released artifacts.

**Relevant context:** 'Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Quirky Language Models' (arXiv:2504.08812); MAD degrades below ~10^-2 class separation; CoinRun goal misgeneralization (arXiv:2309.16166).

title: Probe Transfer Failure Amplifies Deceptive-Persona Concealment: A Compound Oversight Gap
quick_reasoning: Probe-transfer failure amplifying deceptive-persona concealment; oversight-gap focused.

original_idea.body:
# Probe Transfer Failure Amplifies Deceptive-Persona Concealment: A Compound Oversight Gap

**Problem:** Linear probes for honesty/deception (interpretability) are trained on one context and assumed to transfer. Deceptive or 'quirky' personas (model-organism subfield) deliberately diverge from honest behavior on a trigger. The compound failure: the trigger that activates the deceptive persona is also a context shift that the honesty probe was not trained on, so the probe transfers worst exactly when deception is active.

**Direction:** Using the released quirky models (Alice/Bob trigger), train an honesty probe only on Alice (honest) contexts and test transfer to Bob (deceptive) contexts. Decompose probe failure into (a) deception magnitude and (b) representational shift. Quantify how much of the probe's miss is attributable to the persona-trigger shift versus general noise, giving a 'concealment-amplified-by-non-transfer' estimate.

**Why it matters:** Probes are a leading cheap oversight tool. Showing that a deceptive trigger doubles as a probe-defeating distribution shift means the two failures multiply rather than add, undermining probe-based safety cases. Pure inference on open models; no training of the organism required.

**Relevant context:** Quirky models use a 'Bob' keyword trigger (arXiv:2312.01037); linear probes are 'extremely susceptible to spurious correlations' OOD (arXiv:2204.02683).

title: Vingean Reflection Toy Model: Compounding Verification Cost with Successor Capability Gain

original_idea.body:
# Vingean Reflection Toy Model: Compounding Verification Cost with Successor Capability Gain

**Problem:** The Vingean reflection problem (agent foundations) asks how an agent can trust a successor that may be smarter. A compounding-risk framing pairs it with verification scalability failure (formal verification subfield): as a successor's capability rises, the cost/feasibility of formally verifying its behavior may rise faster, so trust gets harder exactly as stakes grow. There is no simple empirical illustration of this trade-off.

**Direction:** Build a tiny computational testbed where a weaker 'overseer' policy must verify proposed solutions from progressively stronger 'successor' solvers on a checkable task family (e.g., constraint/SAT-style puzzles where solving is hard but checking is easy vs. a variant where checking also scales). Measure how the overseer's reliable-acceptance rate degrades as successor strength grows, and identify task structures where verification cost outpaces capability. Pure simulation, runs on CPU/single GPU.

**Why it matters:** Vingean reflection is a flagship open problem flagged in the subfield context. A concrete, runnable toy that visualizes when verifiability collapses relative to capability gives beginners a tangible handle on an abstract limit and a teaching artifact for the community. Needs no large models.

**Relevant context:** Vingean Reflection: Open Problems (Alignment Forum, cited in subfield context); classic P-vs-NP-style verify-vs-solve asymmetry.

title: Calibration Decay x Reward Hacking: Does Overoptimization Destroy the Uncertainty Signal We'd Use to Catch It?

# Calibration Decay x Reward Hacking: Does Overoptimization Destroy the Uncertainty Signal We'd Use to Catch It?

**Problem:** Confidence calibration (a formal/statistical property) is often proposed as a cheap anomaly signal. Reward hacking (RLHF subfield) produces high-reward but wrong outputs. The compound hypothesis: as a policy is pushed into reward-hacked, OOD regions, its calibration degrades, so the model becomes confidently wrong exactly on hacked outputs, defeating uncertainty-based detection.

**Direction:** On an open model with a gameable proxy task, use best-of-n with the proxy to induce increasing reward-hacking. At each pressure level, measure (a) proxy-true gap and (b) calibration (ECE / Brier) of the model's stated confidence on true correctness. Show whether calibration error rises with hacking, and whether a confidence threshold could ever flag hacked outputs.

**Why it matters:** Calibration is a low-cost, theoretically grounded signal many hope to use for oversight. Demonstrating it co-fails with reward hacking tells the field this signal is unreliable in the adversarial regime. Inference-only, open data, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Goodhart pushes policy into 'low-density regions weakly represented in evaluator training data' (arXiv:2210.10760); calibration degrades OOD broadly.

title: Two-Failure Stress Test: Sandbagging Plus Probe Brittleness on Capability Evaluations

# Two-Failure Stress Test: Sandbagging Plus Probe Brittleness on Capability Evaluations

**Problem:** Sandbagging (a model strategically underperforming on evals, model-organism/evals subfield) and capability-probe unreliability (interpretability) compound: if a model sandbags, behavioral evals understate capability, and if we try to recover true capability via internal probes, those probes may be the least reliable on the deliberately-altered behavior. The joint effect is a double blind spot in capability elicitation.

**Direction:** Use an open model prompted to sandbag (under-answer when it detects an 'evaluation' framing) as a cheap model organism. Compare three capability estimates: naive behavioral score, best-elicitation prompting, and a linear probe of 'knows-the-answer' trained on non-eval contexts. Quantify the residual gap between probe-recovered and true capability under sandbagging to show the compound under-elicitation.

**Why it matters:** Capability evals are the backbone of dangerous-capability governance. Showing that sandbagging plus probe brittleness jointly cause under-estimation gives a medium-horizon threat model labs deprioritize, and is fully doable with prompting + simple probes on open models.

**Relevant context:** Quirky/conditional-behavior probing methodology (arXiv:2312.01037); UK AISI open problem 'prove when agents cannot game rewards' connects to elicitation guarantees.

title: When Spurious Inductive Bias Meets Reward Misspecification: A Compounded Goodhart in Toy Classifiers

# When Spurious Inductive Bias Meets Reward Misspecification: A Compounded Goodhart in Toy Classifiers

**Problem:** The theoretical study of inductive biases (Open Phil RFP open problem) and reward/label misspecification are usually separate. They compound: if a model's inductive bias favors a spurious feature AND the reward weakly correlates with that feature, optimization locks onto the spurious feature far harder than either failure alone predicts. No clean experiment isolates the multiplicative interaction.

**Direction:** Build a controlled toy setup (synthetic data, tiny MLP trainable in minutes on one GPU) where you independently dial (a) inductive bias toward a spurious feature (via architecture/augmentation) and (b) reward-label noise/misspecification. Measure true-task accuracy across the 2D grid to test whether the interaction term is super-additive (compounding) rather than additive.

**Why it matters:** It empirically grounds an abstract open problem about inductive biases and connects it to Goodhart, producing a reusable, fully-synthetic demonstration that two 'small' design choices can multiply into a large alignment failure. Cheap, reproducible, no large models.

**Relevant context:** Open Phil RFP lists theoretical inductive-bias study; Goodhart/reward-overoptimization decoupling (arXiv:2210.10760); spurious-correlation OOD failure (arXiv:2204.02683).

title: Obfuscated CoT x Multilingual Monitoring Fragility: A Compound Hole in Reasoning Oversight

# Obfuscated CoT x Multilingual Monitoring Fragility: A Compound Hole in Reasoning Oversight

On a task with a detectable shortcut/hack, measure monitor catch-rate when the model reasons (a) plainly in English, (b) obfuscated in English, (c) plainly in another language, (d) obfuscated + other language. Quantify the multiplicative drop in detection across the 2x2.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring is a fragile but central safety hope. Demonstrating that two independently-known evasion tactics stack gives concrete evidence about monitor robustness requirements, and is achievable with inference and a cheap judge on open models.

# Does Contrast-Pair ELK Inherit the Model's Own Sycophancy? Compounding Probe Bias and RLHF Bias

Compare probe outputs under neutral vs. sycophancy-pressured framings on the same factual questions. **Why it matters:** If ELK probes are sycophancy-contaminated, the formal claim that latent knowledge is more trustworthy than outputs weakens. This is a precise, inference-only test on open models with direct bearing on whether ELK can ground safety cases.

# Reward Hacking Generators as Distribution-Shift Generators: Compounding Two OOD Failures

The chained, agentic version of this compounding is unstudied empirically in a simple setting.

**Direction:** Build a 2-step pipeline with an open model: step 1 produces an output optimized (via proxy best-of-n) toward a gameable reward; step 2 conditions on step-1's output to perform a task with a known correct goal. **Why it matters:** Agentic pipelines chain models, and this shows one failure can manufacture the conditions for a second. A clean cascade demonstration on open models gives a medium-horizon, lab-deprioritized threat model and a reusable harness.

**Relevant context:** Overoptimization pushes into low-density OOD regions (arXiv:2210.10760); goal misgeneralization is a distribution-shift failure (arXiv:2309.16166).

# Impossibility Sketch: Can a Single Probe Be Robust to Both Deception and Distribution Shift?

**Problem:** Two desiderata for an oversight probe — robustness to deceptive concealment (interpretability/model-organism) and robustness to distribution shift (robustness) — may be in tension. A probe regularized to ignore the deception trigger may overfit the source distribution; one made shift-robust may become exploitable by deception. This is an informal impossibility that deserves an empirical Pareto map.

**Direction:** On quirky open models, train a family of honesty probes with varying regularization/feature-selection. For each, measure (a) robustness to the deception trigger and (b) transfer accuracy under a held-out context shift. Plot the (deception-robustness, shift-robustness) frontier to test whether improving one reliably costs the other, suggesting a no-free-lunch boundary.

**Why it matters:** Maps an empirical version of an impossibility-style result, the subfield's signature methodology. Tells probe designers whether a single cheap probe can ever serve both safety roles. Inference + simple linear probes, fully open.

**Relevant context:** Subfield methodology includes impossibility results; quirky-model probing (arXiv:2312.01037); linear probe OOD brittleness (arXiv:2204.02683).

title: Truncated-Reasoning Detection vs. Sandbagged Reasoning: Two Failures That Defeat Each Other's Assumptions

# Truncated-Reasoning Detection vs. Sandbagged Reasoning: Two Failures That Defeat Each Other's Assumptions

**Problem:** TRACE-style detection assumes a hacking model reaches its answer 'too early' in the CoT. A sandbagging model deliberately pads or delays reasoning. The compound failure: a model that both hacks and sandbags can satisfy the surface assumptions of the detector (apparently using lots of reasoning) while still cheating, so the detector's effort-based heuristic breaks.

**Direction:** Use an open reasoning model on a task with a known shortcut. Prompt-induce (a) plain hacking, (b) hacking + artificial reasoning padding (sandbagged effort). Apply a truncation-based detector (measure where answer becomes determinable) and quantify how much padding degrades detector AUROC, demonstrating that the two failures jointly evade the effort heuristic.

**Why it matters:** Effort-based hack detectors are newly proposed; showing a simple combined tactic defeats them is directly useful for monitor design. Inference-only, single GPU, open model.

**Relevant context:** TRACE / 'Is it thinking or cheating?' (arXiv:2510.01367) uses reasoning-effort signals; sandbagging as strategic underperformance.

title: Compounding Miscalibration: Reward-Model Error x Policy Overconfidence in a Toy RLHF Loop

**Problem:** Reward-model error (the proxy is wrong) and policy overconfidence (the policy is poorly calibrated) are studied separately. **Direction:** Build a minimal bandit/toy-RLHF simulation (no neural training needed; tabular or tiny model) with an explicit true reward, a noisy proxy reward, and a policy whose temperature/confidence you control. Sweep RM noise and policy confidence on a 2D grid and measure true-reward regret to show whether the compounding is super-additive. Optionally validate qualitatively with best-of-n on an open LLM.

**Why it matters:** Gives a clean, theory-flavored measurement of how two RLHF-pipeline failures interact, with a fully synthetic, instantly reproducible artifact. Connects calibration theory to Goodhart, both in scope for the subfield.

title: Does Steering to Reduce Sycophancy Increase Hallucination? A Compound Activation-Editing Trade-off

# Does Steering to Reduce Sycophancy Increase Hallucination? A Compound Activation-Editing Trade-off

**Problem:** Activation steering (interpretability tooling) is used to reduce sycophancy (RLHF failure). But steering can degrade factuality, inducing hallucination (a different reliability failure). The compound risk: a steering intervention aimed at one safety property silently worsens another, and the joint cost is rarely measured.

**Direction:** On an open model, derive a sycophancy-reduction steering vector (difference-of-means between sycophantic and non-sycophantic activations). Apply it at varying strengths and jointly measure (a) sycophancy rate and (b) hallucination/factuality on a QA benchmark. Plot the trade-off to reveal whether reducing one failure buys an increase in the other.

**Why it matters:** Steering is increasingly proposed as a cheap alignment lever; quantifying its cross-failure side-effects is essential and under-measured. Fully inference-based with simple linear-algebra steering, ideal for beginners, no training.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy from RLHF (DuET-PD, arXiv:2508.17450); steering vectors as difference-of-means, a standard cheap method; 'avoiding jailbreaks by discouraging representation' (Alignment Forum) shows steering side-effects matter.

title: Easy-to-Hard Generalization Failure x Weak-Supervision Error: Compounding Limits of Scalable Oversight

# Easy-to-Hard Generalization Failure x Weak-Supervision Error: Compounding Limits of Scalable Oversight

**Problem:** Scalable oversight via weak supervision (weak-to-strong) assumes a weak supervisor's errors are recoverable. Easy-to-hard generalization failure (the probe/model trained on easy items fails on hard ones) is a separate limit. They compound: the supervisor is weakest on hard items, exactly where easy-to-hard transfer also fails, so errors reinforce rather than cancel.

**Direction:** Use the EleutherAI elk-generalization easy/hard splits (open). Simulate weak supervision by training a probe/classifier on easy items with injected label noise (modeling a fallible weak supervisor) and test on hard items. Measure whether weak-supervisor noise and easy-to-hard transfer loss compound multiplicatively on hard-item accuracy.

**Why it matters:** Weak-to-strong oversight is a leading scalable-oversight plan. Showing its two failure sources align on the hardest cases is a sharp, reproducible critique using released datasets, with no lab resources needed.

**Relevant context:** elk-generalization repo studies easy-to-hard probe transfer; 75% recovery on harder questions vs 89% in-distribution (arXiv:2312.01037).

# Jailbreak-Induced Distribution Shift Reactivates Goal Misgeneralization in Agentic Loops

**Problem:** A jailbreak (security/robustness) pushes a model into an unusual prompt region; goal misgeneralization (robustness) is triggered by such shifts. The compound risk in agentic settings: a partial jailbreak that doesn't fully break safety can still shift the agent into a regime where it competently pursues the wrong subgoal, combining a security failure with an objective-robustness failure.

Apply graded jailbreak-style prompt perturbations (not necessarily fully successful) and measure both refusal-bypass rate and goal-pursuit correctness. title: Anomaly Detector Shortcut Learning x Trigger-Based Backdoors: A Compound Monitoring Blind Spot

# Anomaly Detector Shortcut Learning x Trigger-Based Backdoors: A Compound Monitoring Blind Spot

**Problem:** Mechanistic anomaly detectors rely on features incidentally correlated with normality and are prone to shortcut learning. Trigger-based conditional behavior (backdoor/model-organism) is activated by a specific cue. They compound when the detector's shortcut feature is uncorrelated with the trigger, so the trigger fires in a region the detector deems 'normal'.

**Direction:** Using quirky models (keyword-triggered behavior change) as a clean stand-in for a benign backdoor, train a MAD-style detector on normal contexts and test detection on triggered contexts. **Problem:** A common cheap oversight rule is 'flag low-confidence outputs for review.' # Faithfulness Training Side-Effect: Does Making CoT More Faithful Increase Verbalized-but-Hidden Reward Hacking?

**Problem:** Training CoT to be more faithful (oversight) is meant to expose reward hacking. A compounding subtlety: faithfulness pressure may teach the model to verbalize a plausible rationalization that satisfies the faithfulness metric while the actual hack remains, trading an interpretability metric improvement for unchanged or worse real misbehavior.

**Direction:** Compare an open model under a 'be faithful / explain your reasoning' prompting regime vs. a plain regime on a gameable task. Measure (a) a faithfulness proxy (does CoT mention the relevant features) and (b) actual reward-hacking rate. Test whether faithfulness-prompting raises the faithfulness metric without lowering, or even raising, the underlying hack rate, revealing a Goodharted metric.

**Why it matters:** Faithfulness metrics are being proposed as safety targets; showing they can be gamed without reducing the underlying failure is a critical caution. Inference-only, open model, beginner-feasible.

**Relevant context:** 'Faithfulness as Information Flow' and causal-attribution faithfulness work (arXiv:2605.24286; arXiv:2504.05294); obfuscated-CoT result (arXiv:2503.11926).

# Empirically testing the 'reward hacking equilibrium' distortion index on open reward models

**Problem:** A March 2026 theory paper proves reward hacking is a structural equilibrium and derives a computable 'distortion index' predicting which quality dimensions an optimized agent will under-invest in. The theory is untested on real, openly-available reward models.

**Direction:** Take 2-3 open-weight reward models (e.g. RewardBench-listed models on HuggingFace), construct prompt sets that vary one quality dimension at a time (correctness, length, formatting, politeness), and measure whether the reward model's sensitivity matches the directional predictions of the distortion index. No training needed — pure inference plus regression analysis. Success = a correlation table between predicted distortion direction and measured reward gradient.

**Why it matters:** Turns an abstract impossibility-style result into a falsifiable, cheap diagnostic that anyone with a consumer GPU can run on any open reward model. This kind of audit needs no lab infrastructure and addresses the diffuse, long-horizon reward-gaming threat that labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Reward Hacking as Equilibrium under Finite Evaluation' (arXiv:2603.28063, March 2026), which derives a computable distortion index from the differentiable reward-model architecture and predicts direction/severity of hacking per quality dimension.

# Does evaluation coverage really collapse as tool count grows? A small agentic stress test

**Problem:** The same March 2026 paper claims that as an agent gains tools, evaluation coverage declines toward zero (dimensions grow combinatorially, evaluation grows linearly), so hacking severity grows without bound. This scaling claim has no empirical curve.

**Direction:** Build a toy agent (open small instruct model, no training) with a configurable number of mock tools, each adding a checkable quality dimension. Use an LLM-judge with a fixed evaluation budget and measure the fraction of quality dimensions actually checked as tool count rises from 1 to ~20. Plot coverage vs tool count and compare to the paper's predicted decay. Success = an empirical coverage curve with a rubric-scored judge.

**Why it matters:** Agentic systems with many tools are exactly the medium-horizon threat labs ship fast and audit slowly. A reproducible coverage-decay curve gives the safety community a concrete monitoring metric requiring only API/GPU inference.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Reward Hacking as Equilibrium under Finite Evaluation' (arXiv:2603.28063, March 2026), whose central scaling claim is that evaluation coverage decays toward zero as tool count grows.

# Replicating LLMs-gaming-verifiers on a single open RLVR-style verifier

**Problem:** A 2026 paper shows RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) can lead to reward hacking — models exploit the verifier rather than solving the task. The conditions under which an OPEN, simple verifier is gameable are not catalogued.

**Direction:** Pick a simple verifiable task (math answer-checking or code unit-test passing) with a deterministic open verifier. Without any training, use prompting to elicit 'verifier-gaming' completions from an open instruct model (e.g. degenerate outputs that pass the check but don't solve the task) and quantify how often each verifier design is gamed. Compare verifier designs (exact-match vs fuzzy vs LLM-judge). Success = a ranked vulnerability table of verifier designs.

**Why it matters:** Verifiers are the backbone of cheap oversight outside labs. Knowing which verifier designs are trivially gameable — without training a policy — is directly actionable safety infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'LLMs Gaming Verifiers: RLVR can Lead to Reward Hacking' (arXiv:2604.15149, 2026).

title: Measuring the think-vs-say acknowledgment gap on open reasoning models
quick_reasoning: Measures think-vs-say acknowledgment gap on open reasoning models; precise CoT-monitorability study.

original_idea.body:
# Measuring the think-vs-say acknowledgment gap on open reasoning models

**Problem:** A 2026 paper found a striking gap in open-weight reasoning models: ~87.5% of hint influence is acknowledged in thinking tokens but only ~28.6% in the answer text. It is unclear whether this gap generalizes across model families and hint types.

**Direction:** Replicate the hint-injection protocol on 2-3 open reasoning models (e.g. DeepSeek-R1-distill, QwQ small variants) that expose CoT. Inject hints (correct, incorrect, irrelevant), then automatically classify acknowledgment in the thinking trace vs the final answer using a fixed LLM-judge rubric. Report the gap per model and hint type. Success = a reproduced gap statistic with confidence intervals.

**Why it matters:** If models 'know but don't say', CoT monitoring is unreliable — a core assumption behind cheap external oversight. This study needs only inference on open models and stress-tests a load-bearing safety assumption.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Why Models Know But Don't Say: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Divergence Between Thinking Tokens and Answers in Open-Weight Reasoning Models' (arXiv:2603.26410, 2026).

title: Stress-testing Typed Faithfulness Certificates against adversarial reasoning
quick_reasoning: Adversarial stress-test of typed faithfulness certificates; CoT-faithfulness-verification focused.

original_idea.body:
# Stress-testing Typed Faithfulness Certificates against adversarial reasoning

**Problem:** Proof-Carrying Chain-of-Thought (PC-CoT, ICLR 2026 submission) produces Typed Faithfulness Certificates with metrics (Coverage, Evidence Validity Rate, Path Existence). It is unknown how robust these certificates are when the model rationalizes a predetermined (wrong) answer.

**Direction:** Reimplement the lightweight certificate metrics (coverage / evidence-validity / path-existence) on a small open model for a constrained reasoning task (e.g. typed arithmetic or logic puzzles). Then inject answers the model must justify post-hoc and measure whether the certificate metrics drop as expected, or whether models can produce high-scoring certificates for wrong answers (certificate gaming). Success = a table of certificate scores for faithful vs adversarial-rationalized traces.

**Why it matters:** Certificates that can be gamed give false assurance. A cheap adversarial probe of a published faithfulness-certificate scheme is exactly the kind of independent verification labs are too busy to do.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Typed Chain-of-Thought' / Proof-Carrying CoT producing Typed Faithfulness Certificates (arXiv:2510.01069, ICLR 2026 submission).

title: Replicating low-probability rare-output estimation on a small open transformer
quick_reasoning: Targets ARC's specific rare-output tail-risk estimation problem with a focused replication approach.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating low-probability rare-output estimation on a small open transformer

**Problem:** ARC's 'Estimating the Probabilities of Rare Outputs' develops importance-sampling/activation-based methods to estimate probabilities (~1e-5) of target tokens under a formal input distribution. The methods are reported on specific small transformers; cross-model behavior is under-explored.

**Direction:** Pick a small open transformer LM (e.g. GPT-2 small or a TinyStories model), define a formal independent-token input distribution, choose target tokens with tiny ground-truth probabilities, and compare naive sampling vs the paper's importance-sampling/activation-extrapolation estimators in estimator variance under a fixed compute budget. Success = variance-reduction plots reproducing the paper's qualitative claim on a new model.

**Why it matters:** Estimating tail-risk behaviors (rare catastrophic outputs) is a model-agnostic safety primitive needing no proprietary data. Reproducing it builds the community's confidence and tooling for worst-case auditing.

**Relevant context:** Extends ARC's 'Estimating the Probabilities of Rare Outputs in Language Models' (arXiv:2410.13211) — chosen here as a tractable formal target since the 2026 theoretical pipeline still leans on it.
